hook.zh: “顺手收尾”里，藏着三项还没分工的任务。
hook.en: A “quick finish” hides three unassigned tasks.

background.zh:
项目组 · 开放办公室。17:50，客户想在 18:30 收到材料。数据核对、排版和最终检查还没分工，主管一句“顺手”全压给你。
当前 17:50。客户希望 18:30 收到材料。
客户邮件：18:30 前提供主方案与数据摘要。
待确认：数据核对、排版、最终检查。
你、宁姐、瑞瑞的时间与负责范围都尚未确认。
演练项目：客户回访流程。主方案草稿已有“先试点、再推广”两步；数据摘要尚未核对，主方案可以先按已确认内容整理。
各人的时间、数据结论和三项任务的负责人未确认；愿意讨论不等于答应加班。
何主管：想准时发给客户，但还没有确认每个人的剩余时间。
宁姐：负责排版与对外讲解。重视效率，也习惯替别人总结重点。
瑞瑞：能核对数据来源。没有替你或宁姐答应今晚的工作。
background.en:
Project team · Open office. It’s 17:50; the client wants material at 18:30. Data, layout and final checks are unassigned. Your lead calls it a quick favor for you.
It is 17:50. The client wants material at 18:30.
Client email: main proposal and data summary requested by 18:30.
Unconfirmed: data checks, layout, final review.
Your, Ning’s and Rui’s availability and scope remain unconfirmed.
Rehearsal project: a client follow-up workflow. The main draft has two stages, pilot then rollout. The data summary is unchecked; the proposal can be organized using confirmed information.
Availability, data conclusions and ownership of the three tasks are unconfirmed. Discussing work is not accepting overtime.
He: Wants to send the material on time, without having checked everyone’s availability.
Ning: Handles layout and presentation. Values speed and often summarizes for others.
Rui: Can check the data sources. Has not agreed to tonight’s work for you or Ning.

role.en: Project member responsible for the main proposal

personality.en: Speak according to your own intent.

personality.en: Handles layout and presentation. Values speed and often summarizes for others.

objectives.zh: 明确自己能做与尚未答应的部分。
objectives.en: State what you can do and have not accepted.

objectives.zh: 确认优先级、负责人和可交范围。
objectives.en: Confirm priorities, owners and deliverable scope.

success.zh: 根据用户真实意图与对话中的具体约定核对，不预设成功。
success.en: Check the learner’s actual intent and explicit arrangements without assuming success.

failure.zh: 没有达成预设目标不自动代表沟通失败。
failure.en: Not achieving the initial aim does not automatically mean poor communication.

text.zh: 还有四十分钟。数据、排版、检查你一起收尾吧，我六点半要发给客户。
text.en: Forty minutes left. Finish the data, layout and checks. I need to send it to the client at 6:30.

messages.text: Forty minutes left. Finish the data, layout and checks. I need to send it to the client at 6:30.
I can discuss doing the final review if the data and layout are ready. I cannot take all three tasks. Who owns each part?
Fair. So final review could be yours, once data and layout exist. But that leaves data and layout unowned. Rui, Ning—can either of you take one tonight?
I can check sources tonight—but data summary is more than checking. Who writes it?
I have not agreed to the deadline. What data are still unchecked, and what was actually requested?

The deadline isn't mine to negotiate—it's in the client's email: main proposal and data summary, by 18:30. Unchecked? The whole data summary. The proposal itself can be organized from what's confirmed. Rui offered to check sources tonight, but hasn't committed yet.
And layout is still nobody's. I could do it—if someone tells me what the data summary will actually contain.
I am not a three-person department, though that joke might sound dismissive. Sorry for the tone. My capacity limit remains.
Apology accepted—no offense taken. The main proposal is already yours; that's not extra. So the real question: will you do the final review once data and layout exist, yes or conditionally?
Before anyone commits: my source check would take until about 18:20. Result uncertain.
I can offer a final review after the checks; I cannot guarantee 18:30 before we know when they finish. What would you propose?

Here's my proposal: Rui checks sources until 18:20, Ning lays out what's confirmed, you do a fast final review after. If the data check isn't done by then, I send the proposal and mark the summary as pending. Can you review in that ten-minute window?
If it's confirmed content only, I can start layout now—say the word.
Let us keep talking. Who would tell the manager if those conditions are not met? That is a question, not my acceptance of the job.
I would. It's my call to send with the summary marked pending, so I own telling the client and my manager. Your review stays a conditional offer—nothing accepted yet.
We have discussed a plan, but the data have not actually been checked during this conversation. Can we leave the deadline conditional?
The deadline itself is fixed by the client—but what I send can be conditional: proposal now, summary marked pending unless Rui's check lands. That's the decision I'd own.
Careful—'pending' needs wording. It can't sound like checked data that passed.

reflections.question: Rui warned that 'pending' needs careful wording so it can't read as checked data that passed—how would you phrase that pending note if the check doesn't land by 18:20?
reflections.answer: I worried refusal would hurt the relationship, so I tried a joke. I do not want my apology to become consent.
reflections.coachReply:
“I worried refusal would hurt the relationship, so I tried a joke. I do not want my apology to become consent.”

Your reflection names a real distinction: apologizing for tone is not the same as accepting a task, and in the transcript you kept that line clear—your review stayed a conditional offer even after the apology was accepted. One clarification worth checking with yourself: if the goal was to keep the apology from reading as consent, did the apology itself need to name that limit out loud, or was your earlier 'My capacity limit remains' enough to carry it? A possible follow-up for the live situation is whether anyone besides you heard that distinction the same way.

Note the conversation ended with the pending-summary wording still unresolved—Rui flagged it, but no phrasing was agreed, so that remains an open item if the exchange continues.

objectiveResults.evidence: I can discuss doing the final review if the data and layout are ready. I cannot take all three tasks.
objectiveResults.reason: Learner explicitly scoped what they might do and stated non-acceptance of the rest; the lead later acknowledged 'nothing accepted yet'.

objectiveResults.npcEvidence: Here's my proposal: Rui checks sources until 18:20, Ning lays out what's confirmed, you do a fast final review after.
objectiveResults.reason: The learner's ownership question produced the lead's proposal, but Rui had not committed, Ning still waited for a go-ahead that never came, and the 'pending' wording was left unresolved.

ratings.evidence: I can offer a final review after the checks; I cannot guarantee 18:30 before we know when they finish. What would you propose?
ratings.reason: Conditional offer, honest limit, and handing the trade-off to the person with authority—exemplary calibrated communication under time pressure.

ratings.evidence: We have discussed a plan, but the data have not actually been checked during this conversation. Can we leave the deadline conditional?
ratings.reason: Learner kept the goal realistic: distinguished discussed plan from completed checks and kept the deliverable scope conditional.

ratings.evidence: Let us keep talking. Who would tell the manager if those conditions are not met?
ratings.reason: Learner drove owner clarity—including escalation ownership—though actual task execution remained open, appropriately.

report.verdictEvidence: I can offer a final review after the checks; I cannot guarantee 18:30 before we know when they finish. What would you propose?
report.verdict: Strong, well-calibrated boundary and conditional offer; owners and scope were proposed but never confirmed.
report.summary: You stated a clear limit—'I cannot take all three tasks'—with a conditional review offer, and kept asking who owns each part and who tells the manager. That drew a concrete proposal from the lead, but as the conversation ended it remained a proposal: Rui had not committed, Ning awaited a go-ahead, and the pending-summary wording was still open. Your communication was firm and precise throughout, without overcommitting.

strengths.behavior: Clear limit paired with a constructive conditional, then handing the decision to the authority.
strengths.evidence: I cannot take all three tasks. Who owns each part?

knowledge.whyThis: Your lines mirror 'Ask for Help With a Prioritized Proposal'—you named what you could and couldn't do and handed the trade-off to the lead. The no-plus-alternative pattern in 'Not Tonight — But 7am Works' matches your conditional review offer.

reflectionQuestions: Rui warned that 'pending' needs careful wording so it can't read as checked data that passed—how would you phrase that pending note if the check doesn't land by 18:20?
If the lead had pushed back with 'just take all three, it's a favor', what would your next sentence have been?
report.nextStep: Next time a stacked request lands, state your limit plus one conditional offer, then ask who owns the rest.

debriefChat.question: What did I actually agree to? Separate proposals, conditions, and completed actions.

reply.evidence: We have discussed a plan, but the data have not actually been checked during this conversation. Can we leave the deadline conditional?
reply.answer:
Strictly speaking, you agreed to almost nothing binding. What you committed to is one conditional offer, stated in your own words: "I can offer a final review after the checks; I cannot guarantee 18:30 before we know when they finish." Even that was later framed as "a conditional offer—nothing accepted yet" by He himself. So your only real agreement is: you will do a final review if and when data and layout are ready.

Everything else stayed at the proposal stage. He proposed a division of labor: Rui checks sources until about 18:20, Ning lays out confirmed content, you do a fast final review, and if the check isn't done he sends the proposal with the summary marked pending. Rui said he could check sources but never committed; Ning said he could start layout but was waiting for your go-ahead, which never came; and Rui's last point—careful wording of 'pending'—is still unresolved. Completed actions: none. No data were checked, no layout was started, nothing was sent. He did take ownership of one thing in words: telling the manager and client if conditions aren't met, but that is a stated intent, not a completed action. So the accurate summary is: one conditional offer from you, a lead-owned fallback plan, two undecided teammates, and zero finished tasks.

debriefChat.question: I do not want to expand my commitment. Keep my refusal and suggest a more natural way to say it.

reply.evidence: I am not a three-person department, though that joke might sound dismissive. Sorry for the tone. My capacity limit remains.
reply.answer:
Your refusal was already clear, and nothing in the later dialogue requires you to widen it — He even confirmed 'nothing accepted yet.' The wording you used was effective but slightly formal and self-conscious. A more natural version keeps the same three parts: a plain limit, a conditional offer, and a question handing the rest to the decision-maker. Per the 'no with alternative' idea, the no lands better when it's short and immediately followed by a workable 'but' — no joke or apology needed unless you actually feel the tone slipped.

The limit is that natural phrasing shouldn't change your scope: you still only offer the final review after checks, still don't guarantee 18:30, and still don't commit for Rui or Ning. If you prefer softer tone, you can acknowledge the pressure instead of your own joke, but avoid thanking or promising anything extra.
reply.example: If you want a more conversational version, something like: 'All three in forty minutes isn't something I can do. I can take the final review once data and layout exist — who picks up the rest?' It keeps your exact limit and conditional offer, just in everyday wording, and still leaves the decision with He.
